key_terms.meaning: 16-bit number that identifies a process on a host; IP address plus port gives a socket address.
IP address combined with a port number, written as IP:port.
Sending many process flows through one IP stream and sorting arriving segments by port.
Transport layer delivers data to the correct application process, not just to the host.
Optional in IPv4 and mandatory in IPv6; detects errors in the UDP header and data.
16-bit field giving the length in bytes of the UDP header plus data.
UDP sends each datagram independently with no connection state at sender or receiver.
32-bit number that labels the first data byte in a TCP segment.
32-bit number giving the next byte the receiver expects; it acknowledges all earlier bytes.
TCP data can flow in both directions at the same time on one connection.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection and agrees on initial sequence numbers.
State held by the endpoint that closes first, long enough to absorb duplicate FINs and old segments.
Window advertised by the receiver; the maximum unacknowledged bytes the sender may have in flight.
Sender-side limit on unacknowledged bytes, grown or cut by TCP congestion control.
TCP starts with a small congestion window and doubles it each RTT until a threshold or loss.
On three duplicate ACKs, TCP resends the missing segment before its retransmission timer expires.
Set of mechanisms that classify, shape, schedule and reserve resources to meet service targets.
Resource Reservation Protocol; a signalling protocol that asks routers to reserve resources for a flow.
Traffic specification in integrated services: token bucket rate, bucket size, peak rate and minimum policed unit.
A connection between two SCTP endpoints that carries multiple independent streams.

takeaways: The transport layer uses port numbers to extend IP host delivery to process delivery; UDP and TCP differ in reliability and state.
UDP adds only ports, length and checksum; it suits short, loss-tolerant messages and applications that build their own reliability.
TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers turn an unreliable packet service into an ordered, reliable byte stream.
TCP connection setup and release use flag exchanges and states; TIME-WAIT protects the close from old duplicates.
Flow control protects the receiver's buffer, while congestion control protects the network.
TCP congestion control uses slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery; loss is treated as congestion.
QoS mechanisms classify and schedule traffic, while integrated services can reserve resources per flow using RSVP and TSpec.
SCTP supports multi-streaming and multi-homing, avoiding head-of-line blocking across independent messages.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually demand a labelled header diagram, a state or sequence trace, and a comparison of UDP, TCP and SCTP or of flow control, congestion control and QoS.

bank.q: Explain how the transport layer turns host-to-host delivery into process-to-process delivery. Define port number and socket address, and show how demultiplexing works at a receiver.
outline: IP delivers to a host; transport delivers to a process
16-bit port number and socket address IP:port
Demultiplexing uses destination port; TCP also uses source IP and source port
Example of several apps on one phone or server

bank.q: Compare UDP and TCP services. Cover connection state, reliability, ordering, message boundaries, flow control, congestion control and typical uses.
outline: UDP is connectionless, unreliable, message-oriented, no flow or congestion control
TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte stream, full duplex
TCP has flow control and congestion control; UDP has neither
Typical uses: UDP for DNS-like short queries, streaming, games; TCP for Web, file transfer, mail

bank.q: Draw the UDP header and explain each field. Why is the checksum optional in IPv4 but mandatory in IPv6?
outline: Four fields: source port, destination port, length, checksum
Length covers header plus data
Checksum covers pseudo-header, UDP header and data
IPv4 allows checksum zero; IPv6 has no IP header checksum, so UDP checksum is mandatory

bank.q: Draw the TCP segment header. Explain the role of sequence number, acknowledgment number, flags, window and checksum.
outline: 20-byte fixed header plus options
Sequence number labels first data byte
Acknowledgment number gives next expected byte and ACK flag makes it valid
Flags SYN, FIN, RST, PSH, ACK, ECE, CWR and window for flow control
Checksum covers header, data and pseudo-header

bank.q: Describe TCP connection establishment with a three-way handshake. Why are two messages not enough?
outline: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number
Server sends SYN-ACK with its own initial sequence number and ACK
Client sends ACK; both sides know the other is reachable and has agreed sequence numbers
Two messages cannot confirm both directions and can accept old duplicate SYNs

bank.q: A TCP sender has bytes 1 to 6000 to send. MSS is 1000 bytes. The receiver advertises a window of 3000 bytes. Show the first four segments and the ACKs, assuming no loss.
outline: Segments carry 1000 bytes each with sequence numbers 1, 1001, 2001, 3001
Window 3000 limits unacknowledged bytes to three segments
ACKs give next expected byte
Sender may send a new segment only after the window opens

bank.q: Trace TCP slow start and congestion avoidance for a connection that starts with cwnd 1 MSS, ssthresh 8 MSS, and loses a segment at round 6. Give cwnd at each round and name the reaction.
outline: Slow start doubles cwnd each RTT until ssthresh
At ssthresh, switch to congestion avoidance and grow linearly
Loss cuts ssthresh and cwnd
Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit and fast recovery; timeout returns to slow start

bank.q: A UDP datagram carries 3000 bytes of payload over IPv4. Explain fragmentation and reassembly at IP, and state what the UDP length and checksum cover.
outline: UDP length is 3008 bytes: 8-byte header plus 3000-byte data
IP fragments the datagram to fit the link MTU
Each fragment has IP identification, fragment offset and more-fragments flag
Receiver reassembles before passing data to UDP; checksum covers UDP header and data with pseudo-header

bank.q: Using RSVP and a token bucket TSpec, describe how an audio flow asks for guaranteed service across three routers. State what each router checks.
outline: Sender sends PATH message with TSpec
Receiver sends RESV message back along the path
Each router performs admission control and reserves bandwidth and buffer
TSpec gives token bucket rate, bucket size, peak rate and minimum policed unit
Guaranteed service provides bandwidth and delay bounds

bank.q: An SCTP association uses two IP addresses at each end. Explain how multi-homing and multi-streaming improve delivery when one path fails and one stream stalls.
outline: Association has multiple streams; loss in one stream does not block other streams
Multi-homing gives primary and backup addresses
Heartbeats detect path failure; SCTP switches to a reachable address
Receiver reassembles each stream independently

bank.q: Analyze why TCP treats packet loss as congestion. Discuss how this assumption fails on wireless links and what mechanisms reduce the problem.
outline: Loss in wired networks usually means queue overflow, so TCP cuts cwnd
Wireless random loss is not congestion; cutting cwnd wastes capacity
Fast retransmit and fast recovery avoid slow start for one loss
ECN can signal congestion before loss; link-layer retransmission hides wireless loss

bank.q: Evaluate the claim: 'UDP is always faster than TCP.' Use header size, connection setup, reliability, congestion control and application needs.
outline: UDP header is 8 bytes; TCP header is at least 20 bytes
UDP has no handshake or connection state
TCP adds ACKs, retransmission, flow control and congestion control
UDP can be faster for small loss-tolerant messages; TCP can be better when reliability is needed
The claim is false in general; speed depends on loss, RTT and application requirements

bank.q: Compare integrated services with simple priority queueing for QoS. Which is easier to deploy at scale, and what does RSVP cost?
outline: Priority queueing classifies packets and serves high-priority queues first
Integrated services reserves resources per flow with RSVP and TSpec
Per-flow reservation gives stronger guarantees but keeps state in routers
Priority queueing is simpler and scales better but gives no firm per-flow guarantee
RSVP cost is signalling, state maintenance and admission control

bank.q: Design a transport choice for (a) live cricket score updates, (b) a UPI payment message, (c) a software download. Justify UDP, TCP or SCTP for each.
outline: Live scores: UDP or SCTP for low delay and tolerance of occasional loss
UPI payment: TCP for reliability, ordering and connection management
Software download: TCP for reliable ordered byte stream and congestion control
SCTP could suit multi-stream messaging but needs support from both ends
Justify with loss tolerance, delay, reliability and message boundaries

glossary.def: TCP flag or number that acknowledges received bytes or a control segment.
Receiver's free buffer space in bytes, carried in the TCP window field.
Network service with no guarantee of delay, loss or bandwidth.
Arithmetic check over header and data to detect bit errors.
TCP phase that grows cwnd by about one MSS per RTT after ssthresh.
Sender's estimate of how many unacknowledged bytes the network can carry.
QoS class that looks like an unloaded best-effort network under normal conditions.
Using a port number to deliver an arriving segment to the right process.
TCP state after fast retransmit that avoids returning to slow start for one loss.
Queue discipline that sends packets in arrival order.
Receiver-driven limit that prevents a fast sender from overflowing the receiver.
Integrated services class with firm bandwidth and delay bounds.
Variation in packet delay; large jitter hurts real-time audio and video.
Maximum segment size; largest TCP data payload a sender may put in one segment.
Combining many process flows into one IP stream using port numbers.
16-bit identifier for a process or service on a host.
Scheduler that serves higher-priority queues before lower-priority ones.
Round-trip time; time for a segment to reach the receiver and for the ACK to return.
Delaying or pacing traffic to keep it within a rate profile.
TCP opening phase where cwnd doubles each RTT until ssthresh or loss.
Endpoint identified by IP address and port number.
Traffic specification that describes a flow's rate and burst parameters for reservation.
TCP state after active close that lasts 2×MSL and protects against old duplicates.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection.
